subject: scripts/db-inventory.mjs

steps.name: the migration chain builds the disposable schema from nothing
the tool reads a live server and calls a chain-built database a match
the aggregates a live server reports for a chain-built database are the chain's own
the chain-built schema answers the founder's digest SQL with the hosted digests
every statement the tool sent is a read
the credential appears in nothing the tool writes or prints
the tool refuses an owner role until --allow-owner is passed
the tool refuses a report path outside docs
a column that no migration created is reported as drift
a table that no migration created is reported as extra
a table the chain requires and the live database lacks is reported as missing
the tool leaves the schema it reads exactly as it found it
the row level security picture the hosted run depends on is produced
the three seeded differences are the whole of what it reports
the digest comparison is sensitive: seeded drift changes all three hashes

notCoveredByDigests: what created the schema (schema_migrations is absent on both)

columnDrift.name: qa_drift_column
columnDrift.problem: present in the live database but created by no migration file

reading: PASS here means the instrument works against a live PostgreSQL server, reads only, keeps the credential out of its report, matches the founder's three canonicalising digests on a schema built only from sql/migrations, and detects drift in both directions and a table count that does not match the chain. It does not mean the hosted beta database was read by this file: styld_beta was never contacted from here, and its digests are the founder's reported values. The run that closes #74 is still the founder's: node --env-file=.env.local scripts/db-inventory.mjs --out docs/readiness/beta/db-inventory.json
digestReading: three identical MD5s, a matching 17.11 and matching 379/106/148 counts mean one thing: under this canonicalisation the public schema of styld_beta and a database built only from these 16 files hold the same columns in the same order with the same types, nullability, defaults and length limits, the same index names with the same definitions, and the same constraint names, kinds and definitions. That is a per-object comparison, not a count, and it is the strongest schema evidence either side has produced. It is still metadata: row data, table or column ownership, grants and ACLs, collation and locale, index build state (indisvalid), tablespaces, storage parameters, extension versions, sequences current values, what created the schema (schema_migrations is absent on both). The digests also say nothing about which role the application connects as, which is #75, and nothing about whether the application enforces the tenant wall itself, which is #76 and the more urgent half now that zero row-level security policies is a measured fact rather than an assumption.
disclosure: the disposable cluster this file owns listens on a loopback port and is destroyed before this receipt is written. Its secret never left the process environment; the report on disk carries host, port, database and role name only, and the per-case reports are removed once their finding is recorded here.
